stimuli.title: Where Soil Carbon Comes From
stimuli.body:
For decades, soil scientists taught that the carbon locked in the world's soils came mainly from decaying plant matter: leaves, roots, and stems that are broken down slowly into a dark, stable substance called humus. On this account, the best way to build soil carbon was to return as much plant residue to the ground as possible, and the long-lived humus molecules were thought to persist because their chemical structure resisted further decay.

Recent work has complicated that picture. Using techniques that trace individual molecules, researchers have found that much of the stable carbon in many soils is not humus at all but the remains of dead microbes, chiefly the cell walls and membranes of bacteria and fungi. Plant litter, it seems, is consumed quickly by microbes, which convert a portion of it into their own bodies. When those microbes die, their remains bind tightly to mineral particles, and it is this attachment to minerals, rather than any molecular toughness, that shields the carbon from further decomposition. Paradoxically, easily digested litter may therefore build more lasting soil carbon than woody litter, because microbes use it more efficiently and so produce more remains per unit of litter.

Defenders of the older view do not deny that microbial remains matter, but they caution that the new finding may partly reflect how carbon is measured. Microbial residues are chemically easy to identify, whereas the complex products of partly decomposed plant material are not, so the latter may be undercounted. Moreover, in forest soils with thick layers of slowly decaying needles, plant-derived carbon appears to dominate regardless of the method used to trace it. A further complication is that soils are rarely uniform, so a handful of samples taken from one field can give a misleading average for the whole.

The disagreement has practical weight. If microbial residues are the key, then farm practices that feed and protect soil microbes, such as planting diverse crops with easily digested roots, deserve priority over practices aimed simply at maximizing the volume of residue left in the field. Yet until measurement techniques converge, the safest conclusion is that soils differ, and that no single recipe for storing carbon will suit them all.

stimuli.title: The Rising Placebo Response
stimuli.body:
In several drug-development programs, patients receiving an inert pill in clinical trials have reported larger improvements in recent years than their counterparts did decades ago. Some analysts take this rising placebo response as evidence that expectations are growing stronger: patients today are better informed, trial sites advertise more heavily, and participants may arrive believing that any treatment on offer is likely to work. If so, new drugs face a moving target, since the gap between drug and placebo can shrink even when the drug's own effect is unchanged.

A different explanation points to the trials themselves. Over time, sponsors have recruited at more sites, many of them paid per enrolled patient, and the pressure to fill places may lead staff to admit people whose symptoms are mild or fluctuating. Such patients tend to improve spontaneously, and because trial ratings are taken only at the start and end, that improvement is credited to the placebo. On this view, what has risen is not the power of belief but the share of participants who would have improved anyway.

The two explanations are not mutually exclusive, yet they carry different advice. If expectations are the driver, trial designers should concentrate on managing what patients are told; if recruitment is, they should tighten eligibility criteria and audit enrollment practices. A sponsor that adopts the first remedy when the second explanation is the true one will spend money and see little change.

stimuli.title: Do Loyalty Programs Build Loyalty?
stimuli.body:
Retailers have long assumed that a loyalty program, which rewards repeat purchases with points or discounts, builds loyalty. Members do spend more than non-members, and the gap is often cited as proof that the program works. But the comparison is weaker than it looks. Customers choose whether to join, and those who already shop frequently at a store have the most to gain from joining. The higher spending of members may therefore be a cause of membership rather than a result of it.

Researchers who have tracked individual shoppers before and after they joined have found a more modest picture. Spending typically rises for a few months and then drifts back toward its earlier level, as members learn to treat the rewards as a discount on purchases they would have made anyway. Programs that pay out only after a high threshold of spending appear to do better, because they give customers a reason to consolidate purchases at one store rather than spread them across several.

None of this suggests that loyalty programs are pointless. Members' purchasing records give retailers detailed data that can guide stocking and promotions, a benefit that does not depend on any change in customer behavior. But a retailer who justifies a program's cost solely by pointing to the higher spending of members is likely to be overestimating its return.

stimuli.title: Faithful to What?
stimuli.body:
Translators of poetry are often told to choose between two loyalties: to the original's words or to its effect. The literalist argues that a translation is a service to the reader who cannot read the original, and that a translator who departs from the words has substituted his own poem for the author's. The recreationist replies that word-for-word fidelity is an illusion. Because every language divides up experience differently, a literal rendering of an idiom or a pun produces something that no reader of the original ever experienced, and so betrays the original's effect while keeping its vocabulary.

Both camps share an assumption that deserves scrutiny: that the original possesses a single fixed effect which a faithful translator could either preserve or lose. Yet readers of the original disagree about its effects, often sharply, and a poem's meaning shifts with each generation of readers. If so, the translator is never choosing between faithfulness and invention but between interpretations, each of which fastens on some features of the original at the expense of others. This does not make all translations equally good. A translation that ignores features a thoughtful reader of the original would notice has failed. But the standard of success is the quality of the interpretation, not closeness to an original effect that never existed in a single form.

stimuli.title: Core Competence and the Outsourcing Maxim
stimuli.body:
In the 1990s, a popular management maxim held that firms should concentrate on their "core competencies" and outsource everything else. The logic seemed unassailable. Specialist suppliers can perform non-core tasks at lower cost because they spread equipment and expertise across many customers, and a firm's managers can then devote their attention to the activities that set the firm apart. Many companies followed the advice, handing to outside contractors functions as varied as payroll, logistics, and component manufacturing.

Experience has been less kind to the maxim than to its logic. Several firms found that an outsourced activity was harder to separate from the core than they had supposed. A maker of consumer electronics, for example, outsourced production of a seemingly generic part, only to discover that small adjustments to the part were needed whenever its own designers altered the product. Each adjustment required lengthy negotiation with a supplier who had little incentive to hurry. The contractor now held the knowledge that the firm needed, and the firm had no easy way to regain it.

Critics of outsourcing conclude from such cases that firms should have kept more activities in-house. That conclusion is too hasty. What the cases show is not that outsourcing is inherently risky but that the "core versus non-core" test is the wrong test. The better question is how easily an activity's requirements can be written into a contract and checked. A task such as payroll, whose output is standardized and whose quality is easily verified, can be handed to a specialist at little risk, even though it is essential to running the business. A task whose requirements change frequently, or whose quality can be judged only by someone who understands the whole product, is hazardous to outsource whether or not it is considered "core."

A firm that merely reverses the old maxim and brings activities back in-house will repeat the original error in mirror image, because it will still be judging by a label rather than by the contract. The sensible discipline is to ask, activity by activity, whether the firm could specify what it wants and tell whether it has been delivered.

stimuli.title: Print and the Spread of Reading
stimuli.body:
A long-standing view among historians holds that the invention of movable-type printing in the fifteenth century caused literacy to spread across Europe. Before printing, books were copied by hand and were expensive; afterwards, they became cheap enough for artisans and merchants to own, and a population that could suddenly acquire books, it is argued, had every reason to learn to read them. The sequence seems so natural that it has often been treated as established fact.

Revisionist historians have pointed out a difficulty with that sequence. Studies of surviving wills, court depositions, and commercial correspondence suggest that literacy was already rising in the commercial towns of several regions decades before the first presses began operating there. Such records are imperfect, since a signature is not the same as the ability to read, but they offer a rough guide to how many people could at least write their names. These historians argue that growing trade created a demand for people who could keep accounts and read contracts, and that printers set up shop in such towns precisely because they already contained many potential readers. On this account, printing was an effect of rising literacy rather than its cause.

The revisionist argument is persuasive as far as it goes, but it treats the question as one of which came first, and that framing may be misleading. Even if early printing followed literacy rather than producing it, it does not follow that printing played no part in the later spread of reading. Printers produced primers and almanacs aimed at readers who could barely read, and the availability of such material may have made it practical for people in the countryside, who had no commercial need to read, to learn. The most plausible account is therefore one of reinforcement: commercial demand began the rise of literacy in the towns, and print then extended it outward, creating more readers, who in turn created more demand for print.

This account fits the evidence better than either simpler story, since it can explain both the early rise of literacy in the towns and its later rise in the countryside.

stimuli.title: How Does Sleep Help Memory?
stimuli.body:
It is widely accepted that sleep helps to consolidate memories, but the mechanism remains disputed. One prominent hypothesis, which its proponents call active consolidation, holds that during deep sleep the brain replays the day's experiences, strengthening the connections between neurons that were active during learning. Evidence cited in its favor includes studies in which volunteers who learned a task in the evening performed better after a night's sleep than after an equal period spent awake.

A rival account, known as synaptic homeostasis, begins from the observation that waking life steadily strengthens connections across the brain, so that by evening many of them are saturated and noisy. Sleep, on this account, does not strengthen the important connections; it weakens all of them proportionally, so that faint ones fall below the threshold of detection while strong ones remain. Memories seem improved after sleep because the clutter surrounding them has been cleared, in the way a signal seems clearer once background noise is reduced.

Both accounts predict that sleep will improve recall, so the behavioral studies cited by one camp cannot settle the matter. What would help is a measurement of what happens to individual connections during sleep. Active consolidation predicts that connections involved in recent learning will grow, whereas synaptic homeostasis predicts that nearly all connections will shrink and that the learned ones will shrink less. Experiments of this kind are technically difficult, and the results so far have been mixed.

stimuli.title: Reflective Roofs and the Urban Heat Island
stimuli.body:
Cities are typically several degrees warmer than their surroundings, a gap known as the urban heat island. Dark roofs and pavements absorb sunlight and re-emit it as heat, and a common remedy is to coat roofs with reflective white paint. Computer simulations suggest that if enough roofs were painted, a city's average summer temperature would fall by a degree or more, reducing both the energy spent on cooling and the incidence of heat-related illness.

Skeptics, however, point to complications that the simulations tend to underplay. A reflective roof sends most of the sunlight that strikes it back into the sky, but the benefit to people depends on where the heat would otherwise have gone. Since most residents spend their time at street level, the cooling of a roof surface matters chiefly to the top floors of a building, whose air-conditioning loads fall. For pedestrians, by contrast, what counts is the temperature of street-level surfaces and of the air near them, and reflective roofs have little direct effect there. Moreover, in cities with cold winters, a white roof that rejects sunlight in July also rejects it in January, so that heating bills may rise by an amount that offsets part of the summer saving.

Some enthusiasts have responded by pointing to the combined effect: when many roofs are coated, the air above the city cools, and this cooler air is eventually mixed down to the street. The response has some force, but only some. Such mixing may be weakest on calm, hot days, which is exactly when cooling is most needed, because still air tends to remain in layers.

A fair reading of the evidence is that reflective roofs are a reasonable investment for particular buildings in particular climates, namely low-rise buildings with large roofs in cities with mild winters, where cooling savings are direct and the winter penalty is small. They are a poor substitute for measures aimed at the street, such as planting trees to shade pavements, which cool the places where people actually walk. City governments that adopt reflective roofs as the central element of a heat strategy are likely to be disappointed.

stimuli.title: What Do Middle Managers Do?
stimuli.body:
A fashionable claim holds that flattening an organization, by removing layers of middle management, speeds decisions and frees employees to use their initiative. The claim has an appealing logic: every layer of review is a place where a proposal can wait, and managers who spend their days relaying information up and down the hierarchy add delay without adding value. Several well-known technology firms have publicized experiments in which whole layers were removed.

Yet the evidence that flatter structures perform better is thin, and some of it points the other way. When a layer is removed, the tasks it performed do not disappear. Someone must still coordinate schedules, resolve disputes between teams, and judge whether individual employees are doing good work. If these tasks fall to the remaining managers, each of whom now supervises many more people, the quality of supervision may decline; if they fall to employees, the very initiative that flattening was meant to release is consumed by administration. Several of the firms that flattened have since quietly reintroduced coordinating roles under new titles.

This is not an argument for tall hierarchies. Layers that merely pass messages along deserve to go. But the lesson is that the useful question is not how many layers a firm has but what work each layer actually does.

stimuli.title: Rotating Antibiotics
stimuli.body:
Bacteria that resist antibiotics are a growing hazard in hospitals, where resistant infections lengthen stays and raise costs, and a long-standing recommendation is that doctors should prescribe antibiotics sparingly, since every course of treatment gives resistant strains an advantage over susceptible ones. In recent years, however, some researchers have proposed an alternative to simple restraint: "cycling," in which a hospital rotates among different antibiotics at fixed intervals, say four months, so that no single drug is used long enough for resistance to it to become entrenched.

Advocates of cycling reason that resistance carries a cost to the bacterium, an idea with elegant appeal because it promises to turn the bacteria's own biology against them. A strain that has acquired resistance to a particular drug typically grows more slowly in the absence of that drug, since the resistance mechanism diverts resources from other functions. If the drug is withdrawn, susceptible strains should therefore gradually outcompete resistant ones, and the drug can be reintroduced later, once its effectiveness has been restored. Early trials of cycling on a handful of hospital wards reported falling rates of resistant infection.

Critics are not persuaded. First, the trials were small, had no control wards, and took place during periods when infection rates were falling for unrelated reasons, so the improvement cannot be confidently credited to cycling. Second, the premise that resistance carries a lasting cost is shaky: bacteria are adept at acquiring compensating changes that remove the cost, so a resistant strain may be at no disadvantage when the drug is withdrawn. Where this has happened, cycling would merely give resistant strains a series of opportunities, one for each drug in the rotation. Third, a patient on a ward is treated with whatever drug is scheduled at the time, not necessarily the one best suited to the infection, which exposes some patients to inferior treatment.

The dispute is unlikely to be resolved by argument. What is needed are larger trials with matched control wards, and until these are completed hospitals would do better to keep to the simpler policy of prescribing sparingly, whose logic is not in dispute.

stimuli.title: Remote Work and Tacit Knowledge
stimuli.body:
As companies have moved to remote and hybrid arrangements, a debate has arisen over whether the office is necessary for learning. Optimists point to studies in which remote workers matched or exceeded the output of office workers in routine tasks such as processing insurance claims or answering customer calls. If output is unchanged, they ask, what has been lost?

The difficulty is that output on routine tasks is a poor measure of what an office provides. Much of what employees need to know is tacit: it is acquired by watching colleagues handle unusual situations, by overhearing how a senior employee frames a problem to a client, or by being corrected informally within minutes of a mistake. Such knowledge does not appear in manuals, and it is transmitted largely as a byproduct of proximity, not through scheduled meetings. A newly hired analyst who sits near experienced colleagues absorbs it without anyone deciding to teach it. Managers sometimes call this "learning the way things are done here," a phrase that captures how little of it is ever written down.

Evidence from a few organizations that tracked new hires over several years is consistent with this concern. Those hired into remote roles were rated as equally competent at the end of their first year, but over the next two years they were promoted less often than comparable employees who worked on site. This is the pattern one would expect if their performance on assigned tasks had been sound while the development of their broader judgment had lagged.

Defenders of remote work reply that these studies describe remote work in its early stages, practiced by firms with no experience of managing it, and that deliberate practices, such as recorded sessions in which senior staff narrate their reasoning, can substitute for proximity. This is plausible, and some firms report success. But such practices must be designed and sustained, and they are exactly the kind of effort that organizations tend to neglect when output figures look healthy. The sensible conclusion is not that remote work is harmful but that its costs are easy to overlook, precisely because the measures most firms use cannot detect them.

stimuli.title: The Debt in the Gift
stimuli.body:
Anthropologists who study gift exchange have long contended that giving is never free. When a person in a small community hands a valuable item to a neighbor, the neighbor is expected to give something back at some later time, and the delay is part of the arrangement: an immediate, equal return would look like a sale and would cancel the relationship that the gift is meant to create. The debt, in effect, is what binds the two parties together.

A recent challenge accepts that gifts create obligations but denies that they are best understood as loans waiting to be repaid. In many of the communities studied, recipients do not keep careful accounts, and a person who has received much from a neighbor over many years may never return anything in kind, yet no one regards the relationship as having failed. What matters, the challengers suggest, is not that each gift be repaid but that the flow of help continues in both directions as circumstances allow. A neighbor who is ill or poor is expected to receive, and the same neighbor is expected to give when able.

The difference is more than a matter of emphasis. On the first view, a community in which some members never reciprocate is suffering a breakdown of obligation. On the second, it may simply be functioning as designed.

stimuli.title: Do Decoys Work Outside the Laboratory?
stimuli.body:
Marketing textbooks routinely describe the "decoy effect": when a seller adds to a pair of options a third, deliberately inferior one, buyers shift toward the option that the decoy makes look better. In the standard illustration, a magazine subscription is offered either at a modest price for digital access alone or at a higher price for digital access plus print. Adding a print-only option priced the same as the combined package makes the combined package look like a bargain, and more people choose it. The effect has been reproduced in laboratory studies in which student volunteers chose among hypothetical products, and it is often cited as a reason for firms to design their price menus with care.

Whether it generalizes to real markets is another matter. Laboratory choices are made quickly, with no budget at stake, among options that are unfamiliar and that differ along only two clearly labeled dimensions. Real shoppers typically know something about the product category, can compare prices across sellers, often research their options for days, and may grow suspicious of a seller when one option looks plainly pointless. Field studies, which are rarer, have produced mixed results: several found no effect, and a few found effects much smaller than in the laboratory.

Defenders of the decoy effect reply that the field studies are unrepresentative because many were conducted in categories, such as groceries, where buyers know prices well and can quickly spot a pointless option. In categories where buyers have little basis for judging value, such as software subscriptions or professional services, they argue, buyers lean on the relationships among the options presented, and the decoy should work. The claim is reasonable but is itself largely untested.

What should a manager take from this? The decoy effect is real in the sense that it can be produced under controlled conditions. Whether it is large enough to be worth designing a menu around in a given market remains an empirical question, one that each firm can answer for itself, at low cost, by running a price test. Even a few weeks of data from a few outlets is often enough to show whether the third option matters.

stimuli.title: Can Oral Testimony Be Trusted?
stimuli.body:
For much of the twentieth century, professional historians regarded oral testimony with suspicion. Memory is fallible, they argued: witnesses forget, embellish, and unconsciously adjust their accounts to fit what they have since learned. A document written at the time of an event, by contrast, was thought to offer a fixed and trustworthy record. The strength of this preference is shown by the fact that for whole periods, especially for people who left few written records, such as laborers, migrants, and domestic servants, history was written almost without their voices.

Advocates of oral history, which became established in the 1960s and 1970s, challenged this view on two fronts. First, they pointed out that documents are not neutral: someone chose to write them, for some purpose, and the writers were often those with power. A document recording a strike, written by the factory owner, is no more objective than the recollections of a striker. Second, they argued that the fallibility of memory is itself informative. When a worker recalls a wage cut as larger than the records show, the discrepancy tells the historian how the event was felt and understood, which a ledger cannot.

Skeptics have not been silenced. They note that it is one thing to say that memory reveals attitudes and another to rely on it for facts, and that oral historians sometimes slide from the first to the second, treating a vivid recollection as proof that events occurred as described. Some skeptics add that interviewers, by the questions they ask, can unwittingly shape the answers they receive. Studies in which recollections have been checked against contemporary records have found that people often remember the broad course of their lives accurately but are unreliable on dates, numbers, and the details of conversations.

A defensible position lies between the two camps. Oral testimony should not replace documents where documents exist and can be checked. But where documents were never made, or were made by a single interested party, it supplies evidence that would not otherwise be had, and the historian's task is to use it for what it can bear, namely the experience and interpretation of events, while corroborating the facts wherever possible.

stimuli.title: Counting People, Making Categories
stimuli.body:
A census appears to be the most straightforward of statistical exercises: it counts the people in a territory and records a few facts about each. Yet the categories in which people are recorded, such as occupation, religion, or ethnic group, are not simply found in the population. What counts as an "occupation" or a "household" must be settled long before the first form is printed; categories have to be defined by the people who design the census form, and the definitions have consequences. A person who must tick one box out of five has been told, in effect, that there are five kinds of person.

Some historians have gone further and argued that census categories do not merely describe social groups but help to create them. Where colonial administrators classified a population into a small number of fixed groups, they say, the groups acquired a reality they had not previously possessed. Officials allocated jobs, schools, and representation by category, and people had reason to organize themselves, and to think of themselves, in those terms. On this view, categories that began as an administrator's convenience hardened into identities.

The argument is illuminating but is sometimes pushed too far. There is evidence that many groups predate the census taker, and that people frequently resisted, ignored, or reinterpreted the categories imposed on them. In several documented cases, large numbers of respondents gave answers that did not fit the available boxes, writing in a different term or leaving the question blank, and so forcing officials to add or merge categories at the next count. The relation between the census and social life, it seems, ran in both directions: official categories shaped how people saw themselves, but people's self-understandings in turn reshaped the categories.

This has a practical lesson for users of census data. Changes in the share of a group from one census to the next cannot be read straightforwardly as changes in the population itself, since they may reflect changes in the definitions, in respondents' willingness to use them, or both. A responsible analyst checks first what the categories meant at each date.

stimuli.title: Forecasting Harvests from Space
stimuli.body:
Forecasts of national crop yields have traditionally relied on surveys: officials ask a sample of farmers how much they expect to harvest. Surveys are slow and costly, and farmers' answers can be biased by the hope of influencing prices. In recent years, analysts have turned to satellite images, which record how green a field appears across the growing season. A greener field generally indicates more vigorous growth, and models that relate greenness to past harvests can produce estimates covering whole countries, weeks before the harvest and at a fraction of the cost.

Satellite-based estimates have their own weaknesses. Greenness measures the quantity of leaves, not the quantity of grain, and the relationship between the two varies with the weather: a hot spell at the time of flowering can ruin the grain of a lush crop. The models also learn from past years, so they perform worst in precisely the unusual seasons, such as a drought following a wet spring, that forecasters most want to anticipate. Finally, in regions with small plots and mixed crops, a single pixel of satellite image covers several fields of different plants, blurring the signal.

Consequently, most agencies that use satellite data treat it as a supplement to surveys, not a replacement. The two sources tend to err in different ways, and an estimate that combines them is more dependable than either alone.

stimuli.title: Photography and the Painter's Eye
stimuli.body:
When photography emerged in the nineteenth century, a familiar story holds, painters were liberated from the burden of recording appearances. The camera could capture a face or a landscape more quickly and exactly than any brush, and painters, no longer needed for this task, turned to what a camera could not do: expressing feeling, distorting form, exploring color for its own sake. On this account, the camera forced painting toward abstraction.

The story is neat, but it is difficult to square with the chronology. Many painters moved away from literal depiction before photography was technically capable of the rapid, detailed work attributed to it; early photographs required long exposures, and portraits often looked stiff and blurred. Moreover, some of the painters most associated with the new styles made extensive use of photographs, as aids for composing scenes and studying movement, and some of them treated the camera as a collaborator rather than a rival.

A more convincing account is that photography changed painting not by taking over a function but by changing what painters could see. A photograph freezes a moment that the eye cannot isolate, such as the positions of a galloping horse's legs, and this revealed to painters that the way things appear in ordinary perception is a construction rather than a plain fact. The effect was not a matter of accuracy alone: it was a matter of seeing what had always been in front of painters but could not be held still long enough to be examined. Having seen how arbitrary the conventions of academic painting were, painters felt freer to invent their own.

Nor was the influence one-way. Photographers imitated the compositions and soft focus of painting to win recognition as artists, which suggests that the two media were in conversation more than in competition. Several photographers of the period also exhibited alongside painters, which further blurred the line between the two trades. The "liberation" story persists because it flatters both parties: it gives the camera a heroic role and relieves painting of any debt to a mechanical device. But a history that sees only competition misses most of what passed between them.

stimuli.title: What Can a Thought Experiment Prove?
stimuli.body:
Philosophers often test theories with thought experiments: imagined scenarios in which a theory is applied to a case that could never occur in practice, and judgments are then sought about what should be said of the case. Suppose a theory holds that what makes a person the same person over time is continuity of memory. A thought experiment might imagine a person whose memories are copied completely into another body, and ask which of the two is the original. The intuition most readers have about such a case is taken as evidence for or against the theory.

Critics, including a number of experimentalists, argue that such intuitions are poor evidence. Surveys show that people's responses to the same scenario vary with trivial changes of wording, with the order in which scenarios are presented, and with the cultural background of the respondent. Some of the variation, moreover, tracks features that have no bearing on the philosophical point, such as the names given to the people in the scenario. If a judgment can be swung by phrasing, the critics ask, why should it be trusted as a guide to the truth?

Defenders reply that the critics' evidence is less damaging than it looks. Variation among untrained respondents reading brief vignettes in a survey, they say, tells us little about the judgments of philosophers who have studied the case closely, considered it from many angles, and learned to notice how a description might mislead. Experts in other fields are also better judges than novices; nobody concludes from the errors of beginners that a chess master's judgment of a position is worthless.

The defenders have a point, but it cannot carry them all the way. The comparison with chess is imperfect: a chess master's judgments can be checked against results, whereas there is no independent way of checking a philosopher's judgment about a case that never occurs. Experience may make philosophers more consistent without making them more correct, since an expert trained in one school of thought may be consistently biased in its favor. The sensible use of thought experiments is therefore as prompts that bring considerations to light, not as tests whose verdicts are decisive.

questions.prompt: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: argue that farming practices should be changed immediately to favor soil microbes
show that the traditional explanation of soil carbon has been decisively refuted
describe a challenge to an established account of how soil carbon is stored and note that the dispute is not yet settled
compare the carbon-storage capacity of forest soils with that of farm soils
explain how techniques for measuring soil carbon have improved over several decades
questions.explanation:
The passage lays out the older view (plant litter becomes humus), then the newer finding (microbial remains bound to minerals), then the objections, and ends by saying soils differ and the safest conclusion is that no single recipe fits all. That is exactly choice C: a challenge to an accepted account, with the dispute left open.

A is too strong: the passage says only that microbial practices "deserve priority" if the new view is right, and the conclusion is cautious. B overstates; defenders of the older view are given real weight. D is out of scope; forest soils appear once, as a qualification. E picks up a single supporting detail (measurement) and makes it the whole point.
questions.tip: For a purpose question, summarize the passage's arc in one sentence before reading the choices, and watch for words like "decisively" or "immediately" that overstate a cautious author.
questions.trap: B is tempting because the new research is described in detail, but the author never says the old view is refuted; the last paragraph explicitly leaves the matter open.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what protects the remains of dead microbes from further decomposition in soil?
choices: Their attachment to mineral particles
The unusual toughness of their cell walls
Their conversion into humus
Their rapid consumption by other microbes
The thick layer of needles above them
questions.explanation:
Paragraph two says that when microbes die "their remains bind tightly to mineral particles, and it is this attachment to minerals, rather than any molecular toughness, that shields the carbon." So A is stated directly.

B is the very explanation the passage rejects ("rather than any molecular toughness"). C confuses the two accounts: humus belongs to the older, plant-based view. D is the opposite of protection, since consumption by microbes is how litter gets turned into microbial bodies in the first place. E refers to forest soils in the final paragraph, where it concerns plant carbon, not microbial remains.
questions.tip: On detail questions, find the exact sentence in the passage and match its wording; the correct answer is usually a close restatement.
questions.trap: B is the trap: toughness was the old explanation for humus, and it is easy to carry it over to the microbial remains by mistake.

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, a proponent of the older account of soil carbon would most likely expect that, other things being equal,
choices: easily digested litter will build more lasting soil carbon than woody litter
microbes play no part in the decomposition of plant litter
most stable soil carbon will be found in the form of microbial cell walls
litter that resists decay will contribute more persistent carbon than litter that is easily digested
the attachment of carbon to mineral particles will be the main factor in its survival
questions.explanation:
The older account held that humus persisted "because their chemical structure resisted further decay." If durability comes from chemical resistance, then litter that is itself resistant should yield more lasting carbon, which is D.

A is the new view's "paradoxical" prediction, so the older view would not expect it. B goes too far; nobody in the passage denies that microbes decompose litter. C is the new finding, not the old. E is also the new view: the mineral attachment is what "rather than any molecular toughness" is contrasted with.
questions.tip: When asked what a rival view would predict, restate that view's mechanism in your own words and then follow it one step forward.
questions.trap: A is attractive because it is the most memorable claim in the passage, but it belongs to the newer theory, so a defender of the older theory would not expect it.

questions.prompt: The author mentions forest soils with thick layers of slowly decaying needles primarily in order to
choices: support the claim that microbial residues are easy to identify chemically
indicate a setting in which the newer finding may not apply, thereby supporting caution about generalizing it
illustrate how plant litter is converted into microbial bodies
show that humus is chemically more stable than microbial residue
argue that measurement methods are unreliable in all soils
questions.explanation:
The sentence begins "Moreover" and sits in the defenders' paragraph, where it adds a second reason for caution: in these forest soils plant-derived carbon seems to dominate "regardless of the method." Its job is to show the newer finding does not hold everywhere, which fits B and the closing remark that "soils differ."

A is a separate point made in the previous sentence. C describes the process in paragraph two, not the forest example. D asserts something the passage never claims. E overreaches on two counts: the example is about forests, and it says the result holds regardless of method, which actually reduces doubt about measurement.
questions.tip: For function questions, ask what claim the example is protecting; here it is the defenders' claim that the new finding is not universal.
questions.trap: E tempts because the paragraph is about measurement, but the forest example is explicitly said to hold "regardless of the method," so it is not an attack on measurement.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best states the main point of the passage?
choices: Placebos have become more effective because patients are better informed than they once were.
Clinical trials should be abandoned in favor of other ways of testing new drugs.
Recruitment practices are the sole cause of the rise in placebo response.
Two explanations for a rising placebo response imply different remedies, so identifying the true cause matters.
New drugs are failing because their own effects are weaker than those of older drugs.
questions.explanation:
The passage offers an expectations explanation, then a recruitment explanation, then says the two "carry different advice" and that picking the wrong remedy wastes money. D captures that structure.

A states only the first explanation as fact. B is never suggested. C is too strong: the author says the explanations are "not mutually exclusive" and never calls recruitment the sole cause. E reverses the first paragraph, which says the gap can shrink "even when the drug's own effect is unchanged."
questions.tip: The main idea of a "two views" passage usually includes both views and the author's comment on them, not just one side.
questions.trap: A and C each grab one explanation and promote it to fact; the author stays neutral between them.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, why might trial staff admit patients with mild or fluctuating symptoms?
choices: Such patients are more likely to believe the treatment will work.
Sites paid per enrolled patient may feel pressure to fill places.
Regulators require trials to include mild cases.
Mild cases make a drug's effect easier to measure.
Better-informed patients ask to join such trials.
questions.explanation:
The second paragraph says that sponsors have recruited at more sites, "many of them paid per enrolled patient, and the pressure to fill places may lead staff to admit people whose symptoms are mild or fluctuating." That is B.

A confuses this with the first explanation (expectations). C and D are not mentioned anywhere. E is a stretch from the first paragraph's "better informed" patients, but the passage links patient information to expectations, not to admission decisions. Always check that the cause named in a choice is the one the passage actually gives for this specific question.
questions.tip: Match the question's "why" to the causal phrase in the passage, here "the pressure to fill places."
questions.trap: A is tempting because belief and expectations dominate the first paragraph, but the second paragraph's mechanism is about who gets admitted, not what they believe.

questions.prompt: Which of the following findings, if true, would most support the second explanation over the first?
choices: Patients in recent trials report higher confidence in new treatments than patients did decades ago.
Placebo response has risen equally at every site, whatever its payment arrangements.
Trial sponsors have spent more on advertising for trial participants.
Drug effects measured against no treatment at all have risen at the same pace as placebo response.
The rise in placebo response is concentrated at newly added sites paid per patient, and is absent at long-established sites.
questions.explanation:
The second explanation says the rise comes from recruitment at paid-per-patient sites admitting people who would improve anyway. If the rise appears only at those new, per-patient sites and not at established ones, that fits the second explanation and is hard to square with a general rise in expectations. That is E.

A and C support the first explanation (stronger expectations, more advertising). B, a rise at every site regardless of payment, would count against the recruitment story. D is irrelevant to the contest, since it compares against a no-treatment group and does not separate the two causes.
questions.tip: To find evidence for one explanation over another, look for a pattern that the first predicts and the second does not, such as where or among whom the effect appears.
questions.trap: A feels supportive because it mentions the trend, but it backs the first explanation, so it cannot favor the second over it.

questions.prompt: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: question a common way of judging loyalty programs while acknowledging that they may have other benefits
prove that loyalty programs have no effect on how much customers spend
recommend that retailers replace loyalty programs with direct discounts
explain why frequent shoppers are more profitable than occasional shoppers
describe how retailers collect data about their customers
questions.explanation:
The first paragraph attacks the member versus non-member comparison, the second reports a more modest effect from before-and-after studies, and the third says programs are not pointless because of the data they yield but that cost justified only by member spending is overestimated. That is A.

B is too strong: spending does rise for a few months. C is never recommended. D is a side detail, not the purpose. E picks up the data point in the last paragraph, but it is one benefit mentioned in passing, not the aim of the passage.
questions.tip: If the author both criticizes and concedes, the right purpose choice will usually contain both moves.
questions.trap: B tempts because the criticism is the loudest part of the passage, but the author explicitly says spending rises at first and that the programs are not pointless.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, studies that follow individual shoppers over time find that, after joining a loyalty program, a member's spending typically
choices: stays at a permanently higher level
falls below its earlier level
rises for a period and then drifts back toward its earlier level
rises only if the program has a low spending threshold
is unaffected from the start
questions.explanation:
The second paragraph states: "Spending typically rises for a few months and then drifts back toward its earlier level." That is C.

A contradicts the drift back. B overshoots: spending returns toward its earlier level, not below it. D reverses the passage, which says high-threshold programs appear to do better. E ignores the initial rise. To check yourself, say the answer aloud as a short before-and-after story: spending goes up, then settles back. Any choice that gives a permanent change, or no change at all, cannot be correct because each one drops half of that story.
questions.tip: Detail questions often test whether you noticed a time sequence; check the "first this, then that" order.
questions.trap: A is the outcome retailers hope for and the one the first paragraph's naive comparison suggests, so it feels familiar even though the passage says otherwise.

questions.prompt: The author mentions the data that purchasing records provide primarily in order to
choices: prove that members spend more than non-members
suggest that retailers should expand their programs
explain why customers choose to join programs
support the claim that spending drifts back toward its earlier level
point to a benefit of loyalty programs that does not rest on changing customer behavior, so that the criticism is not read as a blanket dismissal
questions.explanation:
The final paragraph begins "None of this suggests that loyalty programs are pointless" and then gives the data benefit as the reason, noting it "does not depend on any change in customer behavior." So the function is to qualify the criticism, which is E.

A repeats the weak evidence the author has already questioned. B goes beyond anything stated. C has no connection with data collection. D refers to the second paragraph's research, not the data benefit. A quick test for function questions is to delete the sentence in your head and ask what the paragraph would lose. Without the data point, the final paragraph would read as a flat dismissal of loyalty programs, which the author clearly does not intend.
questions.tip: When a late sentence follows "None of this suggests...", its job is nearly always to limit the scope of the earlier criticism.
questions.trap: B appeals to anyone who reads "benefit" as an endorsement, but the author concludes only that cost is overestimated when justified by member spending, not that programs should grow.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Literal translation is superior to free translation because it respects the author's words.
Free translation is superior to literal translation because it preserves the original's effect.
All translations of a poem are equally valid because readers disagree about the poem.
The usual debate over translation rests on a questionable assumption, and translation should be judged as interpretation.
Translators of poetry should be familiar with the readers of the original language.
questions.explanation:
The author summarizes the literalist and recreationist positions, then says both assume a single fixed effect, argues that translators really choose among interpretations, and sets the standard as the quality of the interpretation. That is D.

A and B each take a side the author declines to take. C is explicitly denied: "This does not make all translations equally good." E is not discussed. In practice, you can often spot this answer by looking for the choice that names the thing the author is questioning and the standard the author proposes in its place. Choices that only take one side of the debate are too narrow to be the main point.
questions.tip: When an author says "both camps share an assumption," the point of the passage is usually to attack that shared assumption.
questions.trap: C is tempting because the author stresses that readers disagree, but the very next sentences block the conclusion that anything goes.

questions.prompt: The first sentence of the second paragraph ("Both camps share an assumption that deserves scrutiny...") serves primarily to
choices: summarize the literalist's argument
introduce a premise that the author goes on to challenge
concede that both camps are correct
provide an example of a poem that has been mistranslated
reject the idea that a translation can ever fail
questions.explanation:
The sentence names a hidden premise that both camps hold, and the rest of the paragraph questions it by pointing to disagreement among readers of the original. So its role is to set up the author's challenge, which is B.

A is too narrow: the sentence concerns both camps. C is the opposite of "deserves scrutiny." D is never done; no particular poem appears. E contradicts the paragraph, which says a translation that ignores noticeable features "has failed." The word "scrutiny" is the clue: authors do not introduce an assumption "that deserves scrutiny" in order to endorse it. When you see language like that, expect the following sentences to test the assumption, and choose the option that says exactly this.
questions.tip: Phrases like "deserves scrutiny" signal that the author is about to challenge, not endorse, the idea just named.
questions.trap: C attracts readers who see "both camps" and assume the author is reconciling them; the author is instead dismantling their shared ground.

questions.prompt: It can be inferred from the passage that the author would most likely agree with which of the following?
choices: Two translations of the same poem could both be successful even though they differ markedly from each other.
The most successful translations are those that depart furthest from the original's wording.
A reader of a translation can judge its success only by also reading the original.
A literal translation can never be a successful translation.
The recreationist is right that fidelity to the original's words is impossible.
questions.explanation:
The author says a translator chooses between interpretations, each of which "fastens on some features of the original at the expense of others," and that success lies in the "quality of the interpretation." If success depends on interpretive quality and not on matching one fixed effect, then different interpretations of the same poem may both succeed, so A follows.

B is not claimed; departing from the words is not a virtue in itself. C brings in a standard the author never states. D is too absolute; a literal rendering may well be a good interpretation. E overstates the recreationist's claim and the author does not endorse that camp, since both camps share the questionable assumption.
questions.tip: For an "author would agree" question, prefer the choice that is the logical consequence of the author's stated standard, and reject extreme words like "never" and "only."
questions.trap: D is the trap: because the author criticizes the literalist's assumption, it feels as if literal translation must be rejected, yet the author criticizes the assumption, not literalness itself.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, why did the electronics manufacturer have difficulty with the part it had outsourced?
choices: The supplier was unable to produce the part at a low enough cost.
The part turned out to be essential to the firm's core competence.
The firm's managers lacked the time to supervise the supplier.
The supplier refused to make any adjustments to the part.
Changes to the product required repeated adjustments that had to be negotiated with a supplier in no hurry to make them.
questions.explanation:
The second paragraph says small adjustments were needed whenever the firm's designers changed the product, and that "each adjustment required lengthy negotiation with a supplier who had little incentive to hurry." That matches E.

A is not stated; cost was the promise of outsourcing, not the problem found. B is tempting but the passage says the part was "seemingly generic," and the difficulty was one of contract and knowledge, not of the part's being labelled core. C is never raised. D overstates: the supplier negotiated slowly, which is different from refusing.
questions.tip: Detail answers restate the passage closely; if a choice adds a new fact such as "refused" or "lacked the time," it is probably unsupported.
questions.trap: B appeals because the story seems to show the part was core after all, yet the author's whole point is that the label "core" is the wrong test.

questions.prompt: The author discusses the maker of consumer electronics primarily in order to
choices: prove that outsourcing is always more expensive than in-house production
show that specialist suppliers are less reliable than internal teams
illustrate a way in which an outsourced activity can prove difficult to separate from the firm's central work
argue that payroll should be performed in-house
demonstrate that the "core competencies" maxim is logically unsound
questions.explanation:
The example opens the paragraph that says an outsourced activity was "harder to separate from the core than they had supposed," and the details (frequent adjustments, a supplier with the knowledge) show exactly that. So C is correct.

A uses "always," which the author rejects in the next paragraph by saying outsourcing is not inherently risky. B is not supported; the supplier's reliability is not at issue. D has no basis in the passage, which says payroll is safe to outsource. E goes too far: the first paragraph says the maxim's logic seemed unassailable, and the second says experience was less kind to the maxim than to its logic, so the example shows a practical difficulty, not that the logic is unsound.
questions.tip: For an example question, find the claim the example sits under; here it is the topic sentence at the start of its paragraph.
questions.trap: E is tempting because the paragraph is critical, but the author attacks the "core versus non-core" test, not the idea that firms benefit from specialist suppliers.

questions.prompt: The author would most likely regard a firm that responded to cases like that of the electronics maker by bringing all of its outsourced activities in-house as
choices: likely to make an error of its own by reclaiming tasks that were safe to outsource
correct in treating outsourcing as inherently risky
wise to have abandoned the idea of specialization
likely to find that its managers can now focus on core activities
certain to regain the knowledge it had lost to its suppliers
questions.explanation:
The last paragraph says a firm that "merely reverses the old maxim" will "repeat the original error in mirror image," judging by label rather than by the contract. Since the author thinks tasks like payroll are safe to outsource, a wholesale return in-house would pull back tasks that did not need to come back. That is A.

B contradicts the claim that outsourcing is not "inherently risky." C is not supported; specialization is not abandoned in the author's view. D is an advantage of outsourcing, not of insourcing. E overstates; regaining knowledge is not guaranteed, and the passage says the firm had "no easy way" to regain it.
questions.tip: When asked how the author would judge an action, find the passage's general principle and apply it, here "judge by the contract, not by the label."
questions.trap: B attracts those who read the author's criticism of the maxim as a verdict that outsourcing is dangerous, but the author calls that conclusion "too hasty."

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, which of the following activities would the author most likely consider safe to outsource?
choices: Manufacturing a component whose design is modified every few weeks by the firm's own engineers
Running a customer-service line whose quality can be judged only by staff who understand the entire product
Designing packaging that must be changed each time the product is revised
Preparing legally required tax filings, whose requirements are fixed by regulation and whose accuracy can be checked against published rules
Writing software whose features cannot be specified until the firm has seen early versions
questions.explanation:
The author's test is how easily the requirements can be written into a contract and verified. D describes a task with fixed requirements and a checkable output, much like payroll, so it is safe even if important.

A matches the electronics example, where frequent changes cause trouble. B matches the passage's second hazard, quality judged only by someone who understands the whole product. C involves constant revision, the same weakness as A. E has requirements that cannot be specified in advance, so it fails the contract test.
questions.tip: Turn the author's criterion into a checklist (fixed requirements, checkable output) and test each choice against it.
questions.trap: C is subtle: packaging sounds peripheral and therefore "non-core," but the author says the label does not matter, and the constant revision makes the contract hard to write.

questions.prompt: According to the revisionist historians, why did printers set up shop in commercial towns?
choices: Paper and ink were cheaper there.
Such towns already had many people who could read.
Country dwellers had asked for primers and almanacs.
Town governments had paid printers to settle there.
The printers themselves had learned to read in those towns.
questions.explanation:
Paragraph two says the revisionists argue that printers set up in such towns "precisely because they already contained many potential readers." Since the towns' literacy had been rising for decades, B is the supported answer.

A, D, and E are never mentioned. C is drawn from the third paragraph, where primers and almanacs reach the countryside, but that is the author's own account, not the revisionists' reason for the printers' location. Notice that the question is limited to what the revisionists argue. The passage has two voices on this topic, the revisionists and the author, and a choice that fits the author's later argument but not the revisionists' reasoning will always be wrong here.
questions.tip: Read the question's subject carefully: "according to the revisionists" restricts you to one paragraph, not the author's view.
questions.trap: C is tempting because it concerns printers' products, but it comes from the author's argument about the later spread of reading, not from the revisionists' reasoning.

questions.prompt: Which of the following findings would be most consistent with the revisionist historians' argument?
choices: Literacy in a town rose sharply only in the years after its first printing press opened.
Printers in a region sold most of their books to country dwellers who had no commercial need to read.
Few records survive from the towns before the presses began to operate.
Printers in several regions closed their businesses because few people could read their books.
Records from a commercial town show growing numbers of signed wills and contracts for several decades before the first press opened there.
questions.explanation:
The revisionists claim literacy was already rising in commercial towns decades before presses arrived. E gives exactly that kind of pre-press evidence, so it is consistent with their argument.

A would support the traditional view that print caused literacy. B supports the author's later point about the countryside, not the revisionists' claim about town literacy preceding printing. C would undermine the evidence base for revisionists. D would suggest that printers misjudged the market, which does not bear on the order of events.
questions.tip: To pick a finding that fits a view, ask what that view predicts about timing or order and look for evidence of precisely that.
questions.trap: A is attractive to readers who see "after the press opened" and think of the passage's main topic, but it favors the traditional view, not the revisionists.

questions.prompt: The author mentions primers and almanacs primarily in order to
choices: support the traditional claim that print caused literacy in the commercial towns
provide evidence that commercial demand for reading did not exist before printing
illustrate a way in which printing might have helped to spread reading even if it did not start the rise in literacy
show that the revisionists have misread the records of wills and court depositions
demonstrate that country dwellers did not wish to learn to read
questions.explanation:
The author has just granted that early printing may have followed literacy; the next claim is that it does not follow that print played no part later. The sentence about primers and almanacs gives the mechanism for that later role: such materials made it practical for rural people to learn. So C is correct.

A is wrong because the author concedes the revisionist point about the towns. B is contradicted by the passage's account of rising demand. D is not argued; the author calls the revisionist argument "persuasive as far as it goes." E gets the countryside backward: the material may have made it practical to learn.
questions.tip: Look at the sentence before an example to see what it is meant to establish; here it is that print may have played a part after all.
questions.trap: A tempts because the author is rehabilitating print, but the rehabilitation concerns the countryside's later rise, not the early rise in towns.

questions.prompt: Which of the following findings, if true, would most strongly support the author's reinforcement account over the revisionists' account alone?
choices: Literacy in the towns rose rapidly only after the presses arrived.
In the countryside, literacy rose faster in villages near printing centers than in otherwise similar villages far from any press, while town literacy had been rising before presses opened.
Literacy rose at the same rate in towns and villages, regardless of whether presses were located nearby.
Printers moved from the countryside to the towns because there were too few readers in rural areas.
Commercial demand for accountants and clerks increased in towns before the first presses were established.
questions.explanation:
The reinforcement account says commerce started literacy in towns and print then extended it outward. To favor it over the revisionist story alone, we need evidence for both stages, and B supplies both: town literacy rose before presses, and rural literacy rose faster near presses. The second fact is what the revisionists alone cannot explain.

A supports the traditional view, since it makes print the starter. C would suggest print made no difference, which favors the revisionists. D is unrelated to the effect of print on rural reading. E, which already fits the revisionist claim, shows only the first stage and does not separate the two accounts.
questions.tip: To favor a combined account over a simple one, look for evidence that supports the extra element the simple account lacks.
questions.trap: E is the trap: it is plainly consistent with the author's story, so it feels right, but the revisionists also predict it, so it cannot separate the two accounts.

questions.prompt: The passage is primarily concerned with
choices: defending the view that sleep consolidates memories by strengthening neural connections
comparing two explanations of how sleep aids memory and indicating what kind of evidence could distinguish them
criticizing researchers who have studied the effect of sleep on volunteers
demonstrating that sleep has no direct effect on the strength of memories
explaining why experiments on neural connections are technically difficult
questions.explanation:
The first two paragraphs introduce the two accounts and the final paragraph says behavioral studies cannot decide between them, then describes the measurement that could. That is B.

A takes the side of one account, but the author presents both neutrally. C is not the tone; the behavioral studies are described as inconclusive, not badly done. D is false, since both accounts agree that sleep improves recall. E mentions a detail from the last sentence, which is not the point of the passage.
questions.tip: When a passage presents two rival accounts and then says what would test them, the main idea usually names both accounts and the test.
questions.trap: A is tempting because active consolidation comes first and gets the sentence about evidence, but position in the passage is not endorsement.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, which of the following is cited as evidence in favor of active consolidation?
choices: Measurements showing that nearly all neural connections shrink during sleep
The observation that waking life saturates connections in the brain
The finding that people recall less after a night's sleep than before it
Volunteers who learned a task in the evening performed better after sleep than after an equal period awake
The fact that background noise is reduced during deep sleep
questions.explanation:
The first paragraph says evidence for active consolidation includes studies in which volunteers who learned a task in the evening "performed better after a night's sleep than after an equal period spent awake." That is D.

A and B are the synaptic homeostasis account's claims. C reverses the finding. E borrows the "background noise" analogy from the second paragraph, where it illustrates how the rival account works; it is not evidence about deep sleep. When the question names a theory, scan only the paragraph about that theory. Here the first paragraph is the active consolidation paragraph, and only one of its sentences mentions evidence, so the answer is easy to locate once you restrict the search.
questions.tip: On "evidence for X" questions, check which paragraph is about X; a choice drawn from the rival's paragraph is almost always a trap.
questions.trap: A feels plausible because it is a specific, technical-sounding claim, but it describes what the rival account predicts.

questions.prompt: Which of the following can be inferred from the author's statement that behavioral studies "cannot settle the matter"?
choices: Improved recall after sleep would be expected whichever account is correct.
The volunteers in the studies did not actually perform better after sleep.
Neither account is able to explain why sleep improves recall.
The behavioral studies were conducted carelessly.
Active consolidation has been shown to be false.
questions.explanation:
The sentence says "Both accounts predict that sleep will improve recall," so a study that finds improved recall fits both accounts and cannot choose between them. A states this directly.

B contradicts the premise: the improved performance is accepted, just not decisive. C is false, since each account does explain it, in different ways. D adds a criticism not in the passage; the studies are limited by what they can distinguish, not by their quality. E overreaches: nothing is said to be false, only that the evidence does not discriminate.
questions.tip: A result that is predicted by both theories has no power to separate them; ask of any evidence, "would the other theory expect this too?"
questions.trap: E tempts those who read "cannot settle" as "disproves," but failing to settle a dispute is not the same as refuting one side.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best states the author's main conclusion?
choices: Reflective roofs are useful in limited circumstances but are overrated as the core of a strategy to protect people from urban heat.
Reflective roofs should be abandoned in favor of tree planting in every city.
Computer simulations of urban heat are unreliable because they ignore winter heating.
Reflective roofs reduce the average temperature of a city by more than a degree.
The urban heat island is caused mainly by dark roofs.
questions.explanation:
The final paragraph gives the conclusion: reflective roofs are "a reasonable investment for particular buildings in particular climates" but "a poor substitute" for street-level measures, and a strategy centered on them will disappoint. That is A.

B is too strong; the author endorses roofs in some cases. C overstates: winter heating is one complication among several, and the simulations are not called unreliable across the board. D is a claim by simulations that skeptics question. E is a background statement in the first paragraph, not the author's conclusion.
questions.tip: The main conclusion is usually signaled in the last paragraph by a "fair reading" or "therefore" sentence; check that your choice keeps both its endorsement and its limits.
questions.trap: B is the extreme version of the author's view and appeals to readers who remember "poor substitute" but forget "reasonable investment" for some buildings.

questions.prompt: The author mentions that a white roof "rejects sunlight in July" and "also rejects it in January" primarily in order to
choices: show that reflective roofs are less effective than dark roofs in all seasons
argue that simulations should model only summer temperatures
explain why heat-related illness is more common in summer
illustrate how roofs absorb sunlight and re-emit it as heat
identify a cost in cold-winter cities that may offset part of the benefit in summer
questions.explanation:
The sentence ends by saying that heating bills "may rise by an amount that offsets part of the summer saving." The July/January contrast is there to show that the same property that helps in summer hurts in winter, which is E.

A is wrong because white roofs are better in summer; the claim is about a trade-off. B is not said anywhere. C is unrelated to the roof argument. D describes dark roofs, the opposite of the reflective roofs under discussion.
questions.tip: Read to the end of the sentence containing an illustration; the purpose is often stated in its final clause.
questions.trap: A is tempting because the sentence is critical of white roofs, but the author concedes they work in summer; the objection concerns winter.

questions.prompt: The passage suggests which of the following about a simulation that projects a one-degree fall in a city's average summer temperature from reflective roofs?
choices: The projection is almost certainly accurate for the city as a whole.
The projection would be higher if the city had cold winters.
Most of the cooling would be felt by pedestrians at street level.
The cooling that people actually experience at street level might be smaller than the projected figure suggests.
The projection would have been reached more reliably by planting trees.
questions.explanation:
The second and third paragraphs say roofs mainly help top floors, have little direct effect at street level, and that mixing of cooler air down to the street may be weakest on hot, calm days. So a citywide average drop need not translate into equal cooling at street level, which is D.

A goes beyond the passage, which questions the simulations' emphasis. B has no support; winter has no bearing on the summer projection. C reverses the skeptics' point. E claims tree planting would make the projection more reliable, a confusion of measures and forecasts.
questions.tip: When an average or aggregate is described, ask who it describes; the passage often hints that a particular group experiences something different.
questions.trap: C is the trap for readers who accept the first paragraph's promise of cooling and forget that the skeptics say the benefit does not reach the street directly.

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, which of the following cities would the author most likely consider the best candidate for a large-scale program of reflective roofing?
choices: A northern city with cold winters whose low-rise warehouses have large flat roofs
A subtropical city of closely packed forty-storey towers whose residents spend most of the day on crowded streets
A subtropical city of low-rise factories and shops with large flat roofs, where the cost of cooling is the main energy expense
A temperate city that plans to coat its roofs instead of planting any street trees
A city with mild winters in which most heat-related illness occurs among pedestrians on shadeless streets
questions.explanation:
The author's last paragraph recommends reflective roofs for "low-rise buildings with large roofs in cities with mild winters," where savings are direct and the winter penalty small. C fits on all three counts: low-rise, large roofs, and a mild-winter (subtropical) climate with cooling as the main energy cost.

A has cold winters, bringing the heating penalty. B is the opposite case: tall towers (the roof is a small part of the building) and pedestrians at street level. D drops tree planting, which the author prefers for the street. E describes a problem at street level, where roofs have little direct effect.
questions.tip: Convert the author's final recommendation into a checklist and eliminate any choice that fails even one item.
questions.trap: E is attractive because the climate is mild and the problem is real, but the author specifically says roofs do little for pedestrians, so the problem described cannot be solved by this remedy.

questions.prompt: The author mentions that several firms have "quietly reintroduced coordinating roles under new titles" primarily to
choices: show that tall hierarchies are more efficient than flat ones
criticize the firms for concealing their mistakes from employees
suggest that the work performed by a removed layer cannot simply be eliminated
demonstrate that employees prefer to have a manager above them
argue that titles matter more than the tasks they describe
questions.explanation:
The sentence closes a paragraph arguing that "the tasks it performed do not disappear." The reintroduced coordinating roles are the evidence: the work still had to be done by someone. That is C.

A is contradicted by the third paragraph ("This is not an argument for tall hierarchies"). B reads "quietly" as an accusation, but the author is only noting a pattern. D is not discussed. E reverses the closing point that what matters is the work each layer does, not its label.
questions.tip: An example at the end of a paragraph usually proves the paragraph's first claim; find that claim and match it.
questions.trap: B takes the word "quietly" too seriously; the author describes the behavior without judging the firms' honesty.

questions.prompt: The passage suggests that the author would be most likely to view the removal of a layer of management as successful when
choices: the layer's work consisted mainly of passing messages along rather than coordinating or evaluating
the remaining managers each supervise many more employees than before
the tasks of the removed layer are transferred to employees as additional duties
the removal is publicized by well-known firms
the firm gives the coordinating roles new titles
questions.explanation:
The author says layers that "merely pass messages along deserve to go" and that the real question is "what work each layer actually does." So removal works best when the layer did little beyond relaying, which is A.

B and C are the two ways the second paragraph says removal goes wrong (poorer supervision or employees swamped by administration). D and E concern publicity and labels, neither of which the author treats as relevant to success. Notice how the answer is built from two separate statements in the passage: layers that merely relay messages "deserve to go," and the real question is what work a layer does. Combining them gives the condition under which removal would succeed.
questions.tip: When a passage ends on a reframed question ("not how many, but what work"), the answer to an inference question usually applies that reframe.
questions.trap: C is the tempting reading for people who recall the first paragraph's promise that employees would be freed, but the second paragraph treats this transfer as a danger.

questions.prompt: Which of the following hypothetical outcomes would most clearly illustrate the second of the two ways, described in the second paragraph, in which the removal of a management layer can go wrong?
choices: Remaining managers each supervise twice as many people, and employees report less frequent feedback on their work.
A firm removes a layer and finds that decisions are made faster and employee satisfaction rises.
A firm retains six layers of management and finds that proposals wait weeks for approval.
A firm gives its coordinators new titles but leaves their duties unchanged.
After a layer is removed, engineers spend several hours each week scheduling shared equipment and settling disputes between teams, and their output of new designs falls.
questions.explanation:
The second paragraph describes two failures: the tasks fall to remaining managers (supervision declines) or they fall to employees, "the very initiative that flattening was meant to release is consumed by administration." E shows engineers losing time to scheduling and dispute-settling, so it fits the second failure.
